corrected_proposal.title: DOJ Drops Proposed Google AI-Investment Divestiture While Seeking Other Remedies
corrected_proposal.description_short: DOJ revised its Google search-case proposal on March 7, 2025, dropping mandatory AI-investment divestiture while retaining a proposed Chrome divestiture.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: On March 7, 2025, the Justice Department filed a revised proposed judgment in the Google search-monopoly case. The proposal dropped mandatory divestiture of Google's AI investments in favor of advance notice for future investments, while retaining a proposed Chrome divestiture and other remedies. Reuters reported that DOJ and 38 state attorneys general continued seeking court relief. This was a change in proposed remedies, not dismissal of the antitrust case or a final court order.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On March 7, 2025, the U.S. Department of Justice and plaintiff states filed a revised proposed final judgment in the federal search-monopoly case against Google. The filing changed the remedies sought: plaintiffs stopped seeking mandatory divestiture of Google's AI investments and instead proposed prior notification of future investments. It maintained other central requests, including Google's divestiture of Chrome, restrictions on search-related payments to distribution partners, and data-sharing provisions. Reuters reported that DOJ and a coalition of 38 state attorneys general still sought a court order requiring Chrome's sale and other measures. The filing was a proposal submitted for the court's consideration; it did not dismiss the antitrust case or establish a quid pro quo. The supplied record's claim that Attorney General Pam Bondi dropped the case after Alphabet made political contributions or held meetings with Donald Trump is not supported by the accessed sources and is excluded. The official filing says plaintiffs changed the AI remedy after additional discovery, but this alone does not prove the rationale or rule out other motives. This corrected entry is limited to the documented procedural change and the remedies still proposed at that point.

corrected_proposal.title: Bondi DOJ Working Group Ordered Review of Federal Actions Involving Alvin Bragg
corrected_proposal.description_short: A February 2025 DOJ memo directed a working-group review that included alleged federal cooperation with Alvin Bragg’s Trump prosecution.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: On February 5, 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi created the DOJ Weaponization Working Group and directed it to review federal enforcement activity from the previous four years. The memo included alleged federal cooperation with Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s Trump prosecution among the subjects for review. It did not establish that allegation, announce a Bragg-specific criminal investigation, or find that Bragg acted improperly.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On February 5, 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi issued a memo establishing the Justice Department’s Weaponization Working Group. The directive assigned the group a review of federal civil and criminal enforcement activities during the previous four years and called for quarterly progress reports to the White House. Its list of topics included what the memo called “federal cooperation with the weaponization” by Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg, New York Attorney General Letitia James, their staffs, and other New York officials against Donald Trump and his businesses. That language states the administration’s allegation and the subject of a review; it is not a finding that Bragg coordinated with federal authorities or acted unlawfully. The memo also does not announce a criminal investigation into Bragg. The frozen entry’s claim that DOJ opened a February investigation into Bragg, along with its assertions about Bragg’s cooperation and a coordinated campaign against prosecutors, is not supported by the material reviewed and is omitted. The documented event is the DOJ review directive concerning the earlier Trump prosecutions.

corrected_proposal.title: Federal Court Blocks Trump's Order Targeting the Minority Business Agency
corrected_proposal.description_short: EO 14238 directed MBDA to sharply reduce functions; a federal court later preliminarily enjoined implementation after staff and grant actions.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: Trump signed Executive Order 14238 on March 14, 2025, directing the Minority Business Development Agency to eliminate nonstatutory functions and reduce statutory operations and staffing to the legal minimum. The Rhode Island federal court later recorded that most MBDA staff were placed on leave and grants appeared terminated, then granted a preliminary injunction. This account corrects the February date and does not claim all federal minority-business support ended.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On March 14, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14238, directing the Minority Business Development Agency to eliminate nonstatutory functions to the maximum extent allowed by law and reduce statutory work and staffing to the legal minimum. Afterward, MBDA placed all but five employees on paid administrative leave, and the district court said the agency appeared to have terminated its existing grants. In its May 6 preliminary order, the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island stated that the executive order, as carried out, violated the Administrative Procedure Act in an arbitrary and capricious way and disregarded Congress’s role in authorizing agencies and appropriating funds. The court granted a preliminary injunction against implementing the order at MBDA. That was a preliminary ruling, not a final merits judgment. The records do not show that all federal minority-business support or SBA programs ended, or establish later agency operations after the injunction.
organization_tags: U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island

source_fact_map.fact: EO 14238 was signed March 14, 2025 and directed MBDA to eliminate nonstatutory functions and reduce statutory functions and staff to the minimum required by law.

It also disregards the fundamental constitutional role of each of the branches of our federal government; specifically, it ignores the unshakable principles that Congress makes the law and appropriates funds, and the Executive implements the law Congress enacted and spends the funds Congress appropriated.

And now, those five employees have since been reassigned to positions outside the MBDA. ECF No. 35-4 ¶ 5. MBDA also announced that it was implementing a RIF. ECF No. 1-3. And the agency appears to have since terminated all preexisting MBDA grant awards in furtherance of the Reduction EO.

The Defendants oppose the motion on various jurisdictional grounds and assert that the States have not satisfied the elements required for entitlement to preliminary relief. evidence_map.source_excerpt: Plaintiffs are twenty-one states (the “States”) who move for a preliminary injunction, seeking to restrain the Defendants from implementing the President’s Executive Order 14238, “Continuing the Reduction of the Federal Bureaucracy” (“Reduction EO”), as it applies to three federal agencies—the Institute of Museum and Library Services (“IMLS”), the Minority Business Development Agency (“MBDA”), and the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (“FMCS”). The Defendants oppose the motion on various jurisdictional grounds and assert that the States have not satisfied the elements required for entitlement to preliminary relief. For the reasons stated below, the Court GRANTS the States’ motion.

A nationwide agency was affected; the preliminary injunction interrupted implementation, and no private benefit is shown.
